extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, classics, education, and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative and prescriptive principles from a close, academic reading of Plato's Republic and related dialogues about education, art, and political life. Focuses on doctrines that bear on how literature, education, and artistic practice ought to be shaped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first principle which runs through all art and nature is simplicity; this also is to be the rule of human life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity is a guiding rule across music, gymnastic, law, and medicine; Plato and the author advocate simplicity over overcomplication, urging that greater matters be decided simply and that regulation avoid unnecessary complexity. The passage links aesthetic simplicity to moral and political simplicity (e.g. restoring law to common sense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false sentiment in drama for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: “He is afraid too of the influence of the drama, on the ground that it encourages false sentiment, and therefore he would not have his children taken to the theatre; he thinks that the effect on the spectators is bad, and on the actors still worse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato would exclude theatrical material that fosters false or corrupting sentiment from children's education; specifically the author notes banning the 'lusts and treacheries of the gods' and misbehaving Homeric heroes as models. The guidance implies evaluating dramatic content by its moral and formative effects on youth and restricting exposure accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the false before the true (education by figure)
rubrics_metrics.description: “He must be taught the false before he can learn the true.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's pedagogical paradox: early instruction may present simplified or mythical versions (‘false’) as preliminary vehicles for grasping higher principles (‘true’). The author adds that modern educators would limit fiction's use to what necessity requires, but acknowledges teaching by figure is defensible when aimed at inculcating principles rather than facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as lifelong, holistic preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Education is to comprehend the whole of life, and to be a preparation for another in which education begins again.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should not be a finite apprenticeship but a continuous thread through life—beginning anew at different stages—integrating moral, intellectual, and physical training. The Republic’s scheme is presented as encompassing infancy (elsewhere), youth, active life, and later contemplative study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate abstraction (mathematics as organon)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The great aim of education is the cultivation of the habit of abstraction. This is to be acquired through the study of the mathematical sciences.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato prizes mathematical study because it trains the mind to grasp universals and relations, preparing it for dialectic and the idea of the Good. The author acknowledges limits—mathematics’ true bounds were not known then—but stresses its role in shaping abstract thinking and intellectual discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster individuality and genius (avoid systems that smother)
rubrics_metrics.description: “...a system which, instead of fostering the scattered seeds or sparks of genius and character, tends to smother and extinguish them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique of Sparta and of overly regimented political/social systems: creative and political institutions should avoid suppressing remarkable individuals. Progress of cities/nations often arises from remarkable individuals; therefore systems that enforce uniformity are to be judged negatively for stifling genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use artistic analogies to clarify virtue, but beware literalness
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the virtues as yet presented no distinct conception to the mind, a great advance was made by the comparison of them with the arts; for virtue is partly art, and has an outward form as well as an inward principle. The harmony of music affords a lively image of the harmonies of the world and of human life...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies (music→virtue, art→ethics) can give definiteness and elevate notions of government and duty; they are valuable rhetorical and pedagogical tools. However, the author warns that such analogies can be specious if treated as literal equivalences—one must distinguish instructive image from factual truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false or specious analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: “Analogies, though specious as arguments, may often have no foundation in fact.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and thinkers should not allow vivid analogies to substitute for sound argument. Plato is criticized here for drawing over-hasty analogies (state↔individual); the recommended practice is careful analysis to ensure analogical reasoning is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance bodily and intellectual training
rubrics_metrics.description: “He affirms that music and gymnastic are not... intended, the one for the cultivation of the mind and the other of the body, but that they are both equally designed for the improvement of the mind... Two points are noticeable... the time of training is entirely separated from the time of literary education.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should harmonize physical and intellectual development rather than overemphasize one at the expense of the other. The author disputes Plato’s strict separation of bodily training and literary education, warning that prolonged exclusive bodily training could harm intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention via education rather than remedial excision
rubrics_metrics.description: “The true remedy for them is not extirpation but prevention. And the way to prevent them is to take care of education, and education will take care of all the rest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addressing social ills (disease, vice, legal confusion), prioritize preventive measures—particularly broad, formative education—over punitive or excisional remedies. For cultural/creative policy, emphasize structures that cultivate good dispositions early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fiction to instill moral principles but limit harmful content
rubrics_metrics.description: “He would make an entire reformation of the old mythology... The lusts and treacheries of the gods are to be banished... The principles on which religion is to be based are two only: first, that God is true; secondly, that he is good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myth and fictional material may be reworked to serve moral education: retain elements (e.g., Homeric strain that teaches endurance) that form character, while removing corrupting models. Aim fiction toward inculcation of basic moral truths and good taste rather than sensational or corrupting portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value visionary abstractions despite current vacuity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The IDEA of good... is apt to be regarded by the modern thinker as an unmeaning abstraction; but he forgets that this abstraction is waiting ready for use, and will hereafter be filled up by the divisions of knowledge.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High metaphysical or abstract ideals (even if presently vague) can motivate inquiry, frame future classification, and influence conduct. Creative and philosophical work can responsibly deploy grand abstractions as guiding ends while recognizing their provisional nature.
